workshops.title: arc42 in a Day
workshops.headline: Architecture documentation that people and AI can act on.
workshops.lead: arc42 is a free, open template for documenting software architecture. One hands-on day to write yours, for engineers at every level.
workshops.format: In person, in teams of 3 to 4

price.label: TT$999
price.standardNote: After that, the standard price is confirmed by email.

workshops.affiliation: This workshop is independent. It is built on the free arc42 template, which was created by Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka, and is not affiliated with or endorsed by arc42. It does not lead to a certification.
sections: Why does it exist, and what matters most?

why.pull: AI tools can generate code, but they can’t read your intent. Documentation that records goals, contracts and decisions is how you hand it over.
what: arc42 is a free, open template for documenting software and system architecture. Its twelve sections give each kind of architecture information a clear place: goals and constraints, context, building blocks, runtime behaviour, deployment, crosscutting concepts, decisions, quality scenarios, risks and a glossary.
It is a structure, not a method, and it doesn’t care about notation: Markdown, text-based diagrams or UML all work. It fits well as docs-as-code, kept in the repository and reviewed like source.
It is free to use, even commercially, with credit to its creators, Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka.

now.text: People leave, systems grow and decisions fade. A consistent structure makes the why findable.

now.lead: AI tools only know what is written.
now.text: Coding agents generate code quickly but guess at intent. Goals, contracts and recorded decisions are how you give it to them.

now.lead: Specifying and checking are gaining value.
now.text: As more code is generated, stating what good looks like and verifying the result become the scarcer skills.

goals.how: AI coding tools start every session knowing nothing about your project. Without a written map they read lots of files and guess, and you pay for every token. A short, accurate architecture note (what the parts are, what each promises, what you decided and why) gives them what the code can’t tell.
goals.ws: You write the short version: a strategy table, block descriptions, one contract and one decision record. Then you test it with a prompt template and a simple three-way experiment.
goals.real: The evidence is mixed. A February 2026 ETH Zurich study reported that long, auto-generated context files lowered success and raised cost by over 20%. So the aim is short, human-written and specific, not more. Test it on your own tasks.

goals.h: Build systems and integrations with fewer surprises
goals.how: Most integration trouble hides at the edges: who talks to whom, in what format, and what happens when it fails. arc42 gives you a context view, interface contracts, failure scenarios and decision records, so colleagues and vendors work from the same picture.
goals.ws: You draw the context and Level-1 views, write a contract with error modes, and trace one runtime scenario with a failure branch.
goals.real: It won’t design the system for you. It makes your design visible so it can be questioned before it is expensive to change.

goals.h: Turn an idea into a brief anyone can build from
goals.how: Founders and freelancers need to explain an idea to developers, clients and AI tools without it being misread. Quality goals, constraints such as budget, team and deadline, and a context view turn a vague idea into something others can build, price and challenge.
goals.ws: Use your own idea as the workshop case if you like. You leave with goals, constraints, a context view and a list of risks.
goals.real: A document doesn’t prove people will pay. Use it to sharpen the idea, then test the market.

goals.h: Build the skills AI makes more valuable
goals.how: As AI writes more of the code, the scarce skills move towards deciding structure, stating what good looks like, spotting AI’s mistakes and recording why. Those are the skills this workshop practises.
goals.ws: In the AI lab, AI drafts sections from your notes, then your team red-teams the result and decides what to keep.
goals.real: This builds skill, not a job guarantee. You practise judging AI output, which stays useful whatever tools change.

workshops.dayIntro: Each part has a finished example and then your turn. You build one document across the day: your own arc42 skeleton, section by section, for a real system your team knows.

day.title: Opening
day.text: Why architecture goes undocumented, how we will learn, and the rules for using AI today. Form teams, choose your system and set up your tools, then take a short baseline quiz you will retake at the end.
day.tag: You leave with: a team, a case and a working arc42 file

day.title: Foundations
day.text: What architecture is, why it is a set of trade-offs, and what good documentation is not. Stakeholders and concerns, views, the C4 zoom levels, and the twelve arc42 sections. A quick Markdown and Mermaid warm-up.

day.title: Section 1: goals, quality and stakeholders
day.text: Write a requirements overview that names no technology, then turn vague qualities like “fast” and “secure” into scenarios with numbers. Find the stakeholders and what each expects.

day.title: Section 2: constraints
day.text: Sort constraints from decisions from requirements with the three-question test, then write your own numbered constraints.

day.title: Section 3: context and scope
day.text: Treat your system as a black box. Draw the business context, then record the technical channels in an interface table.

day.title: Section 4: solution strategy
day.text: Turn each quality goal into an approach, a reason and the trade-off you accept. A neighbour reads only your table and guesses your architecture.

day.title: Section 5: building blocks
day.text: Split the system into five to nine blocks, name their responsibilities and interfaces, then write a contract with pre-conditions, post-conditions, invariants and error modes for your riskiest block.
day.tag: Exercises 5a and 5b · Level-1 view and one contract

day.title: Sections 6 to 8: runtime, deployment, crosscutting
day.text: Draw one scenario as a sequence diagram with a failure branch, map every block to where it runs, and name the rules that recur across blocks.

day.title: Section 9: decisions
day.text: Write an architecture decision record with real alternatives and at least one honest negative consequence, so a new teammate understands why not the other option.

day.title: Sections 10 to 12: quality, risks, glossary
day.text: Grow your quality tree with a change scenario and a failure scenario, then list risks with mitigations and owners, and define your terms once.

day.title: AI lab
day.text: Have an assistant draft sections from your notes. Then red-team the result for ignored instructions, contradictions between sections and unsupported claims, and repair it, giving every AI line a verdict.

day.title: Agents as readers
day.text: What humans and coding agents each need from documentation: short indexes, contracts, stable IDs and reasons. Turn an invariant into a test, and see how to check the effect on your own work.

day.title: Close
day.text: Check your skeleton against a checklist, walk the gallery, retake the quiz, rate your own progress and leave with a 30-day plan.
day.tag: You leave with: a complete first-draft arc42

leave.title: A complete skeleton

facilitator.name: A practising architect
facilitator.role: Solution architect and workshop facilitator, Intellica
facilitator.bio: Your facilitator has spent three decades turning complicated software and process ideas into things teams can actually use. As a solution architect, they have worked across Oracle, IBM, Microsoft, EMC, HP, Cisco and NetApp platforms on major system implementations throughout the Caribbean, and have explained difficult concepts in workshops for decades, including three years lecturing computer science in the mid-2000s. Today they lead Intellica’s work designing and operating production AI systems documented with arc42, C4 and architecture decision records, so that any team can pick up the build on day one.

faq.a: A free, open template with twelve sections for writing down how a software system is built and why. It was created by Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka.

faq.q: Is this the official arc42 training?
faq.a: No. This is an independent workshop built on the free arc42 template. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by arc42, and it does not lead to a certification.

faq.q: I’m an experienced engineer. What’s in it for me?
faq.a: The template is the easy part. The depth is in measurable quality scenarios, contracts with invariants and error modes, decision records with real alternatives, an AI lab where you red-team generated documentation, and designing docs that coding agents can use without drifting.

faq.q: I’m new to this. Will I keep up?
faq.a: Yes. Every section starts with a finished example, early exercises are mostly filled in, and you work in a team. The support fades as you gain confidence.

faq.q: Will this really cut my AI costs?
faq.a: It can, if you keep the documentation short and specific. Evidence so far is mixed, and long auto-generated context files can make things worse. The workshop shows you how to test the effect on your own work.

faq.a: No. Boxes, arrows and plain words are enough.

workshops.sources: arc42: docs.arc42.org. On context files for AI coding agents: a February 2026 ETH Zurich study (Gloaguen et al.) reported that long, LLM-generated context files lowered task success and raised inference cost by over 20%, as summarised by Little Bear Apps. Other analyses report benefits from concise, human-written files. Findings are early and vary by tool and task, so we teach you to test on your own work.

guide.skeleton:
# <System name> — arc42 skeleton
## 1. Introduction and Goals
### 1.1 Requirements overview
### 1.2 Quality goals (top 3–5, each with a scenario)
### 1.3 Stakeholders (role, expectation)
## 2. Constraints (ID, constraint, why, effect)
## 3. Context and Scope
### 3.1 Business context (diagram)
### 3.2 Technical context (table)
## 4. Solution Strategy (goal, approach, why, trade-off)
## 5. Building Block View
### 5.1 Level 1 (diagram + table)
### 5.2 Contract: <block>
## 6. Runtime View (scenario + failure branch)
## 7. Deployment View (environments, mapping table)
## 8. Crosscutting Concepts
## 9. Architecture Decisions (ADR-0001…)
## 10. Quality Requirements (tree + scenarios)
## 11. Risks and Technical Debt
## 12. Glossary
guide.mermaid:
```mermaid
graph LR
  A[Customer] --> B[Order app]
  B -->|HTTPS| C[Payment provider]
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Customer->>App: place order
  App-->>Customer: confirmation
```
terms: A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in the system. A concern is something they care about, such as recovering a lost order.
A testable statement of stimulus, response and metric, such as “95% of confirmations appear within 3 s at 300 orders per minute”.
A container is something you start: an application or data store. A component is a grouping of related functionality behind an interface inside a container.
What a block promises and expects: pre-conditions, post-conditions, invariants and error modes.
An architecture decision record: one significant decision with its context, options, decision and consequences.
Repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once.
guide.aiRules: Write a human draft first. Then ask AI why, and what’s missing, not only to write it. You decide: give every AI line a verdict of accepted, rejected or edited, with a reason. Use only your workshop case, and never paste passwords, keys, personal data or client-confidential details.
before: Every quality goal has a scenario with a number
Every block in section 5 traces to a strategy or goal
At least one ADR with an alternative and a negative consequence
IDs (C1, ADR-0001) are referenced somewhere else
guide.thirty: Week 1: finish sections 1–4 with your real team. Week 2: sections 5–6, one contract per critical block. Week 3: three ADRs, five scenarios, risks. Week 4: try the agent experiment (no docs, a short index plus two contracts, or the full arc42) and share what you find.

evidence: Retrieval practice and spacing are well studied, but the size of the effect varies. A 2024 study across nine STEM courses found a small average gain from spaced retrieval (about two percentage points) and not in every course (Bego and colleagues, International Journal of STEM Education). We use both because they cost you little, not because they guarantee a result.

example.title: Doubles-to-Go: a worked example you can read and run
example.lead: The workshop teaches with one small, real system: a pre-order app for street-food vendors in Trinidad. You get its complete arc42 document and a working app built to match it, so you can see each section turn into code, and watch the design cope when things go wrong.

parts.title: The arc42 document
parts.text: All twelve sections: goals, constraints, context, strategy, building blocks with three contracts, runtime scenarios with failure branches, deployment, crosscutting concepts, six decisions, eleven quality scenarios, eight risks and three items of technical debt. Every one has a stable ID.

parts.title: The working app
parts.text: One small Node service with no dependencies, plus plain web pages for customers and vendors. The payment provider and SMS gateway are faked inside it, so everything runs offline on your laptop.

parts.title: Tests that guard the document
parts.text: 33 tests check the contracts, the quality scenarios and the block boundaries. A checker fails if the arc42 uses an ID it never defines. Documentation and code are kept honest by the build.

parts.title: An agent guide
parts.text: A short AGENTS.md tells a coding agent where to start, which rules never bend and which commands to run. It is the “agents as readers” idea, made concrete.

run: npm test       # 33 tests: contracts, scenarios, architecture rules
npm run simulate   # 1,000 customers with dropped connections
npm run docs:check # the arc42 checks its own consistency (needs python3)
